paragraph: Ayodhya was to look dazzlingly beautiful decked with flowers, perfumed by sandalwood and incense. The streets were to be sprinkled with water and made lively by dancers and singers dressed richly, while temples were to be stocked with food and alms. Sumantra was sent to fetch Rama from the palace. The king watched his son so very dear to him, approach looking like the lord of the gandharvas. Mighty armed, beautiful of countenance with eyes large like the soft lotus petals, he captivated the hearts of all those that beheld him. His presence made them delirious with joy. Alighting from the chariot, Rama advanced towards the palace that shone like the peaks of mount Kailash. With palms held together he bowed to his sire saying, 'I, Rama, have come,' and prostrated to Dasaratha touching his feet with reverence. The king then embraced Rama and sat him on a seat made of gold encrusted with the most precious of gems, on which was cast the brilliance of Rama's self-effulgence. "My son, offspring of the best of my queens, you are the most cherished of my children. Virtuous that you are, you have won the hearts of your people. Accept the throne of Ayodhya. Though you blemishless, my boundless love for you makes me give counsel, for your benefit. Let neither love nor anger sway you. Keep your ministers and subjects happy. Granaries and arsenal must be well stocked. To you the love of your people is as important as the nectar of immorality is to the gods. Always be calm with all your senses under control and never indulge in acts that generate greed or anger. Be ever aware of all happenings in the country." Friends of Rama hurried to Kausalya to convey the glad tidings and the queen filled with joy, gifted them with cows, gold and jewels. Rama adored and worshipped by the thronging crowds took leave of Dasaratha reverentially and retreated to his abode. The assembled crowds, who were happy their wishes were gratified, prayed to the gods for a coronation without obstructions.
Chapter/Canto/Verse_Reference: Ayodhya Kanda, Sarga 3 (Rama is Summoned and Dasaratha's Counsel)
Situation/Problem_Faced: Ayodhya is being prepared for the grand coronation. Rama is summoned by Dasaratha, who then formally offers him the throne and provides extensive counsel on the duties of a king, emphasizing virtues like impartiality, wisdom, and public welfare. Kausalya receives the joyful news, and the people express their fervent hope for a smooth coronation.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage highlights the ideal characteristics of a righteous king through Dasaratha's counsel to Rama, emphasizing impartiality, welfare of subjects, control of senses, and constant vigilance. It also showcases Rama's humility and reverence despite his divine qualities. The widespread public adoration for Rama and their prayers for an obstruction-free coronation underscore the collective hope and trust placed in him, setting a high expectation for his reign. The festive atmosphere and gifts signify the joy and auspiciousness surrounding the event.
Outcome/Resolution: Ayodhya is prepared for the coronation, with decorations and provisions. Rama is summoned by Dasaratha, who formally offers him the throne and provides detailed advice on virtuous and effective kingship. Kausalya rejoices and gives gifts. Rama then reverentially takes leave, and the people pray for an unobstructed coronation, full of anticipation.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Raja Dharma (King's Duty - the detailed counsel given by Dasaratha to Rama)
Seva (Service - Rama's dedication to his people's welfare)
Indriya Nigraha (Control of Senses - key advice from Dasaratha)
Pranama (Reverential Bowing - Rama's respect for Dasaratha)
Dharma (Righteousness - the underlying principle of Rama's character and proposed rule)
Prajaranjana (Keeping the Subjects Happy - a core tenet of good governance)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The passage details the 'Mangala' (auspicious) preparations for Rama's coronation. Dasaratha's counsel to Rama focuses on 'Raja Dharma' (king's duty), emphasizing virtues like 'Indriya Nigraha' (sense control) and prioritizing the 'welfare of his people'. Rama's 'Pranama' (reverential bowing) to his father and the people's prayers for an 'obstruction-free coronation' underscore the deep spiritual significance of this event, seeking divine blessings for Rama's reign of 'Dharma'.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, the passage exudes collective joy and fulfillment as Ayodhya prepares for Rama's coronation, a widespread sentiment that makes people 'delirious with joy'. Dasaratha's counsel to Rama reflects deep paternal love and wisdom, focusing on the psychological traits of a good ruler: emotional regulation, empathy ('delve into the hearts of men'), and a lack of ego and anger. Rama's humility and the people's adoration highlight harmonious social relationships and a collective sense of well-being, while their prayers for a smooth coronation reveal a shared hope and the psychological need for security in leadership.
